'''Morris Tanenbaum''' (November 10, 1928 – February 26, 2023) was an American physical chemist and executive who worked at [[Bell Laboratories]] and [[AT&T Corporation]].

Tanenbaum made significant contributions in the fields of [[transistor]] development and [[semiconductor manufacturing]]. Although it was not made public at the time, he developed the first [[silicon]] transistor, demonstrating it on January 26, 1954, at Bell Labs.<ref name="Milestone">{{cite journal|title=First Transistor IEEE Milestone Dedication|url=https://web.njit.edu/~ieeenj/archived_newsletters/2009_12.pdf|access-date=11 February 2018|journal=IEEE Newsletter |volume=56|issue=5|publisher=North Jersey Section of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers|date=2009|quote=Dr. Tanenbaum had a distinguished career starting at Bell Labs where he worked under Shockley and made the first silicon transistor.}}</ref><ref name="Friedman">{{cite news|last1=Friedman|first1=Alexi|title=N.J. scientist honored for invention that paved way for digital age|url=http://www.nj.com/business/index.ssf/2013/11/jobs_gatestanenbaum_nj_scienti.html|access-date=11 February 2018|work=The Star-Ledger|date=November 10, 2013}}</ref> He also helped develop the first gas-diffused silicon transistor, which convinced Bell administrators to prefer the use of [[silicon]] rather than [[germanium]] in their transistor design. He later led a team that developed the first high-field [[superconducting magnet]]s.

Later in his career he became an executive. He dealt with the [[Breakup of the Bell System|separation of Bell Laboratories and AT&T]], and became the first chief executive officer and chairman of the board at [[AT&T Corporation]] on January 1, 1984.

==Early life and education==
Morris Tanenbaum was born to Ruben Simon Tanenbaum and Mollie Tanenbaum, on November 10, 1928, in [[Huntington, West Virginia]], US. Tanenbaum's parents were [[Jewish]], and had emigrated from Russia and Poland, first to [[Buenos Aires]], Argentina and then to the United States. Ruben Tanenbaum owned a [[delicatessen]].<ref name="Transcript">{{cite book|first1=David C. |last1=Brock|first2=Christophe|last2=Lécuyer|title=Morris Tanenbaum, Transcript of an Interview Conducted by David C. Brock and Christophe Lécuyer at Bell Telephone Laboratories, Inc. Murray Hill, New Jersey on 3 May and 26 July 2004 |date=26 July 2004 |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/sites/default/files/tanenbaum_m_0668_suppl.pdf|place=Philadelphia, PA|publisher=[[Chemical Heritage Foundation]] }}</ref>

Morris Tanenbaum attended [[Johns Hopkins University]], earning his bachelor's degree in [[chemistry]] in 1949.<ref name="OH"/>
As a [[sophomore]] at Johns Hopkins University, Tanenbaum became engaged to his future wife Charlotte Silver<ref name="OH"/> in September 1949, after his graduation from Johns Hopkins.<ref>{{cite news|title=Tanenbaum Silver|quote=Mr. and Mrs. Harry M. Silver, of Shirley avenue, have announced the engagement of their daughter, Miss Charlotte Marilyn Silver, to Mr. Morris Tanenbaum, son of Mr. and Mrs. Reuben Tanenbaum, of Callow avenue. Mr. Tanenbaum is engaged in graduate study at Princeton University.|date=September 18, 1949|url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/217005816/|work=The Baltimore Sun|page=60|place=Baltimore, Maryland}}</ref>

Encouraged by professor Clark Bricker, who was himself moving, Tanenbaum went from Johns Hopkins to [[Princeton University]] for his doctoral work. There he first studied [[spectroscopy]] with Bricker. He then did his thesis work with [[Walter Kauzmann]], studying the properties of metal [[single crystal]]s. Tanenbaum received his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in chemistry from Princeton in 1952 after completing a doctoral dissertation titled "Studies of the [[Deformation (engineering)|plastic flow]] and annealing behavior of [[zinc]] crystals."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tanenbaum|first=Morris|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/2791846|title=Studies of the plastic flow and annealing behavior of zinc crystals|date=1952|language=English}}</ref><ref name="OH">{{cite web|author=Center for Oral History| title= Morris Tanenbaum |url=https://oh.sciencehistory.org/oral-histories/tanenbaum-morris|website= [[Science History Institute]] }}</ref><ref name="Goldey">{{cite web|title=Oral-History:Goldey, Hittinger and Tanenbaum|url=http://ethw.org/Oral-History:Goldey,_Hittinger_and_Tanenbaum|website=Engineering and Technology History Wiki|access-date=9 February 2018}}</ref>

==Career==
Morris Tanenbaum joined the chemistry department at [[Bell Telephone Laboratories]] in 1952. He held a number of positions at Bell, beginning in the technical staff from 1952 to 1956, becoming assistant director of the metallurgical department until 1962, then director of the solid-state development laboratory until 1964. He was executive vice-president for systems engineering and development from 1975 to 1976.<ref name="OH"/>

Tanenbaum then moved to the [[Western Electric Company]], where he worked as director of research and development (1964–1968), vice president of the engineering division (1968–1972) and vice president of manufacturing: transmission equipment (1972–1975).<ref name="OH"/>

He returned to Bell Laboratories in 1975 as vice President of engineering and network services from 1976 to 1978. He served as president of the [[New Jersey Bell Telephone Company]] from 1978 to 1980, then returned to Bell Laboratories as Executive Vice President for Administration from 1980 to 1984.<ref name="OH"/> On January 16, 1985, he was appointed "corporate executive vice president responsible for financial management and strategic planning".<ref name="Gilpin">{{cite news|last1=Gilpin|first1=Kenneth N.|title=BUSINESS PEOPLE; 4 Senior Officers Shifted at A.T.&T.|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/01/17/business/business-people-4-senior-officers-shifted-at-at-t.html|access-date=9 February 2018|work=The New York Times|date=January 17, 1985}}</ref> Concerns that AT&T and Bell Laboratories effectively held a [[monopoly]] on [[communication technology]] throughout the United States and Canada led to an [[United States antitrust law|antitrust case]], ''[[United States v. AT&T (1982)|United States v. AT&T]]'', and the eventual [[breakup of the Bell System]]. Tanenbaum was closely involved in discussion of related senate legislation, and helped to draft the proposed "Baxter I" amendment.<ref name="Temin">{{cite book|last1=Temin|first1=Peter|last2=Galambos|first2=Louis|title=The fall of the Bell system : a study in prices and politics|date=1989|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge [England]|isbn=0521389291|edition= 1st paperback |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CXNPVjdxfAEC&pg=PA241}}</ref>

Following the restructuring, Tanenbaum became the first chief executive officer and chairman of the board at [[AT&T Corporation]] from 1984 to 1986.<ref name="NAP2001">{{cite book|author=Committee on Science, Engineering, and Public Policy, National Academy of Sciences, National Academy of Engineering, Institute of Medicine, Policy and Global Affairs|title=Implementing the Government Performance and Results Act for research : a status report|date=2001|publisher=National Academy Press|location=Washington, D.C.|isbn=978-0-309-07557-2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ICG0xmbQjqQC&pg=PA52|access-date=12 February 2018}}</ref> From 1986 to 1988 he served as AT&T's Vice Chairman for Finance, and from 1988 to 1991, AT&T's vice chairman for finance and chief financial officer.<ref name="OH"/>

==Research==
When Tanenbaum joined the chemistry department at [[Bell Laboratories]] in 1952, Bell was a hotbed for semiconductor research. The first [[transistor]] had been created there in December 1947 by [[William Bradford Shockley]], [[John Bardeen]] and [[Walter Houser Brattain]]. Their [[point-contact transistor]], a block of the semiconductor [[germanium]] with two wires touching it, was announced at a press conference in New York City on June 30, 1948.<ref name="Riordan"/><ref name="Hoddeson"/>

Finding better semiconductor materials to support the "transistor effect" was a critical area of research at Bell. [[Gordon Teal]] and technician Ernest Buehler did pioneering research on the growing and doping of semiconductor crystals between 1949 and 1952.<ref name="Riordan"/> Teal's group built the first [[Grown-junction transistor|grown-junction germanium transistors]], which were announced by Shockley at a press conference on July 4, 1951.<ref name="SE">{{cite web|title=1951: First Grown-Junction Transistors Fabricated|url=http://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/first-grown-junction-transistors-fabricated/|website=Computer History Museum |publisher=The Silicon Engine|access-date=12 February 2018}}</ref> Meanwhile, [[Gerald Pearson]] did important early work investigating the properties of silicon.<ref name="Riordan">{{cite journal|author1-link=Michael Riordan (physicist)|last1=Riordan|first1=Michael|title=The Lost History of the Transistor|journal=IEEE Spectrum|date=30 April 2004|url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/the-lost-history-of-the-transistor|access-date=12 February 2018}}</ref>

Tanenbaum's initial work at Bell focused on possible [[single crystal]] Group [[Boron group|III-V]] [[semiconductor]]s such as [[indium antimonide]] (InSb) and [[gallium antimonide]] (GaSb).<ref name="InSb">{{cite journal|last1=Tanenbaum|first1=M.|last2=Briggs|first2=H. B.|title=Optical Properties of Indium Antimonide|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_physical-review_1953-09-15_91_6/page/1560|journal=Physical Review|date=15 September 1953|volume=91|issue=6|pages=1561–1562|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.91.1561.2|bibcode=1953PhRv...91.1561T}}</ref>

===The first silicon transistor===

In 1953, Tanenbaum was asked by Shockley to see if transistors could be made using [[silicon]], from group [[Carbon group|III-IV]].<ref name="Tanebaum">{{cite web|first=Morris|last=Tanebaum|title=First-Hand:Beginning of the Silicon Age|url=http://ethw.org/First-Hand:Beginning_of_the_Silicon_Agem|website=Engineering and Technology History Wiki|access-date=12 February 2018}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Tanenbaum built on Pearson's research, and worked with technical assistant Ernest Buehler,<ref name="Gertner">{{cite book|last1=Gertner|first1=Jon|title=The idea factory : Bell Labs and the great age of American innovation|date=2013|publisher=Penguin Books|location=London|isbn=978-0143122791|page=380|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OkECDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA380}}</ref> whom he described as "a master craftsman in building apparatus and growing semiconductor crystals."<ref name="Riordan"/> They used samples of highly purified silicon from [[DuPont]] to grow crystals.<ref name="Riordan"/>

On January 26, 1954, Tanenbaum recorded a successful demonstration of the first silicon transistor in his logbook. However, Bell Laboratories did not publicise Tanenbaum's discovery—the successful transistor had been constructed using a rate-growing process,<ref name="Valdes">{{cite journal|last1=Tanenbaum|first1=M.|last2=Valdes|first2=L. B.|last3=Buehler|first3=E.|last4=Hannay|first4=N. B.|title=Silicon n‐p‐n Grown Junction Transistors|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_journal-of-applied-physics_1955-06_26_6/page/686|journal=Journal of Applied Physics|date=June 1955|volume=26|issue=6|pages=686–692|doi=10.1063/1.1722071|bibcode=1955JAP....26..686T}}</ref> which was felt to be poorly suited to large-scale manufacturing. Diffusion processes, pioneered by Bell's [[Calvin Fuller]], were seen as more promising. Tanenbaum became the team leader for a group studying the possible application of diffusion to the fabrication of silicon transistors.<ref name="Riordan"/>

In the meantime, [[Gordon Teal]] had moved to [[Texas Instruments]], where he was essential to the organization of TI's research department. He also led its team of silicon transistor researchers. On April 14, 1954, he and [[Willis Adcock]] successfully tested and demonstrated the first grown-junction silicon transistor. Like Tanenbaum, they used highly purified DuPont silicon. Teal was able to bring the silicon transistor to production. He announced the results and displayed the TI transistors on May 10, 1954, at the [[Institute of Radio Engineers]] (IRE) National Conference on Airborne Electronics, in [[Dayton, Ohio]].<ref name="Riordan"/>

===The first gas-diffused silicon transistor===
By 1954, several researchers at Bell Labs were experimenting with diffusion techniques to create layered semiconductors. Charles A. Lee developed a germanium semiconductor using diffused [[arsenic]] in late 1954.<ref name="Morton">{{cite book|last1=Morton |first1=David L. Jr.|last2=Gabriel|first2=Joseph|title=Electronics : the life story of a technology|date=2007|publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press|location=Baltimore, Md.|isbn=978-0801887734|pages=58–59|edition= Paperback |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8NAxnNNpxDQC&pg=PA58|access-date=12 February 2018}}</ref>
Meanwhile Tanenbaum worked with Calvin Fuller, D. E. Thomas, and others to develop a gas diffusion method for silicon semiconductors.<ref name="Holonyak">{{cite journal|last1=Holonyak|first1=Nick|title=The origins of diffused-silicon technology at Bell Labs, 1954-55|journal=The Electrochemical Society Interface|date=2007|volume=16|issue=3|pages=30–34|doi=10.1149/2.F03073IF|url=https://www.electrochem.org/dl/interface/fal/fal07/fall07_p30-34.pdf}}</ref><ref name="CHI">{{cite web|title=1954 - Diffusion Process Developed for Transistors|url=http://www.computerhistory.org/siliconengine/diffusion-process-developed-for-transistors/|website=Computer History Museum |publisher=The Silicon Engine|access-date=12 February 2018}}</ref><ref name="Thomas">{{cite journal|last1=Tanenbaum|first1=M.|last2=Thomas|first2=D. E.|title=Diffused Emitter and Base Silicon Transistors |journal=The Bell System Technical Journal|date=1956|volume=35|issue=1|pages=1–22|url=https://archive.org/details/bellvol35systemtechni00amerrich|access-date=12 February 2018|doi=10.1002/j.1538-7305.1956.tb02371.x}}</ref>
Fuller developed a way to expose thin slices of crystalline silicon to gaseous [[aluminum]] and [[antimony]], which diffused into the silicon to form thin multiple layers.<ref name="Gertner"/> Tanenbaum needed to establish a reliable electrical contact with the middle layer.<ref name="Friedman"/>{{rp|169–170}}

After weeks of experimenting, Tanenbaum wrote in his laboratory notebook on March 17, 1955, "This looks like the transistor we’ve been waiting for. It should be a cinch to make."<ref name="Friedman"/>{{rp|169–170}}
The diffused-base silicon transistor was able to amplify signals at frequencies above 100 megahertz, with a switching speed 10 times faster than previous silicon transistors.
The news convinced executive Jack Andrew Morton to return early from a trip to Europe and adopt silicon as the material for the company's future transistor and diode development.<ref name="Missed">{{cite journal|last1=Riordan|first1=Michael|title=How Bell Labs Missed the Microchip|journal=IEEE Spectrum|date=1 December 2006|volume=43|issue=12|pages=36–41|doi=10.1109/MSPEC.2006.253406|s2cid=24238492|url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/how-bell-labs-missed-the-microchip|access-date=12 February 2018|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="Gertner"/><ref name="Memorial">{{cite book|last1=National Academy of Engineering|title=Memorial Tributes|date=1979|publisher=The National Academies Press.|location=Washington, D.C.|volume=1|chapter=Jack Andrew Morton|chapter-url=https://www.nap.edu/read/578/chapter/42|access-date=12 February 2018|doi=10.17226/578|isbn=978-0-309-02889-9}}</ref>

In 1956, with financial backing from [[Arnold Beckman]], William Shockley left Bell Labs to form [[Shockley Semiconductor]]. Shockley made Tanenbaum an offer but Tanenbaum chose to stay with Bell Labs.<ref name="OH"/> The [[NPN transistor|n-p-n silicon transistors]] created with the double-diffusion method were referred to as "[[mesa transistor]]s" as they had a raised area or "mesa" above the surrounding layers of etching.<ref name="Hoddeson">{{cite book|author1-link=Michael Riordan (physicist)|author2-link=Lillian Hoddeson|last1=Riordan|first1=Michael|last2=Hoddeson|first2=Lillian|title=Crystal fire : the birth of the information age|date=1997|publisher=Norton|location=New York|isbn=978-0393041248|pages=[https://archive.org/details/crystalfirebirth00rior/page/223 223]|url=https://archive.org/details/crystalfirebirth00rior/page/223}}</ref> The initial goal at Shockley Semiconductor was to fabricate prototype n-p-n silicon transistors, based on the "mesa" structure pioneered by Tanenbaum and his co-workers at Bell Labs.<ref name="transfer"/> By May 1958 Shockley's employees had successfully met that goal.<ref name="transfer">{{cite journal|last1=Riordan|first1=Michael|title=From Bell labs to silicon Valley: A saga of semiconductor technology transfer, 1955-61|url=https://www.electrochem.org/dl/interface/fal/fal07/fall07_p36-41.pdf|journal=The Electrochemical Society Interface|date=2007|volume=16|pages=36–41|issue=Fall|doi=10.1149/2.F04073IF}}</ref>

Bell Laboratories did not take advantage of Tanenbaum's early achievements by capitalizing on the possibilities of chip technology. They became increasingly dependent on other companies for microchips and [[large-scale integrated circuit]]s.<ref name="Missed"/> Tanenbaum expressed disappointment at this missed opportunity.<ref name="OH"/>

===High-field superconducting magnets===
After becoming Assistant Director of the Metallurgical Department at Bell Labs in 1962, Tanenbaum led a group doing basic research into applied metallurgy. [[John Eugene Kunzler]] was interested in the electrical properties of commercially important metals at low temperatures.<ref name="OHMT">{{cite web|title=Oral-History:Morris Tanenbaum|url=http://ethw.org/Oral-History:Morris_Tanenbaum|website=Engineering and Technology History Wiki|access-date=9 February 2018}}</ref>
[[Rudy Kompfner]] was trying to build [[maser]] amplifiers to detect and measure very low microwave signals, and needed high magnetic fields to tune his masers. Kunzler tried developing superconducting coils to meet Kompfner's needs, using lead-bismuth alloys drawn into wire and insulated with copper. He was able to produce record-setting magnetic fields of one or two thousand [[Gauss (unit)|gauss]], but they were not high enough for Kompfner's use.<ref name="OHMT"/><ref name="Rogalla"/> Berndt Matthias had discovered that a brittle ceramic-like material, [[Nb3Sn]], compounded of [[niobium]] and [[tin]], could superconduct at a higher temperature than previous superconductors.<ref name="Matthias">{{cite journal|journal = [[Physical Review]]|volume = 95|issue = 6|pages = 1435|year = 1954|title = Superconductivity of Nb<sub>3</sub>Sn|url = https://archive.org/details/sim_physical-review_1954-09-15_95_6/page/1434|first1 = B. T.|last1 = Matthias|last2 = Geballe|first2 = T. H.|authorlink2 = Theodore H. Geballe|last3 = Geller|first3 = S.|last4 = Corenzwit|first4 = E.|doi = 10.1103/PhysRev.95.1435|bibcode = 1954PhRv...95.1435M}}</ref>

Tanenbaum worked with technician Ernest Buehler to develop a way to form the Nb3Sn compound into a coil and insulate it. He credits Buehler with the idea behind their PIT (powder in tube) approach. They sought to avoid Nb3Sn's fragility issues by delaying the point at which the material was formed: 1) combining a mixture of ductile, pure niobium metal and tin metal powders in the proper ratio, 2) using it to fill a tube formed from a non-superconducting metal such as copper, silver or stainless steel, 3) drawing the composite tube into a fine wire which could then be coiled and 4) finally heating the already-coiled tube to a temperature at which the niobium and tin powders would react chemically to form Nb3Sn.<ref name="OHMT"/><ref name="Rogalla">{{cite book|last1=Rogalla|first1=Horst|last2=Kes|first2=Peter H.|title=100 years of superconductivity|date=2012|publisher=CRC Press/Taylor & Francis Group|location=Boca Raton|isbn=978-1439849460|pages=644, 663–667|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fnbRBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA662}}</ref>

On December 15, 1960, their first day of testing, Tanenbaum and Kunzler's group tested the high field properties of a rod of Nb3Sn that had been fired at 2400°C. It was still superconducting at 8.8 T, their maximum available field strength.<ref name="Rogalla"/> Tanenbaum had wagered Kunzler a bottle of [[Scotch whiskey]] for every .3T reached above 2.5T, so this outcome represented an unexpected 21 bottles of Scotch. Testing PIT strands resulted in even more powerful effects.<ref name="Rogalla"/>{{rp|644}}<ref name="Kunzler">{{cite journal|last1=Kunzler|first1=J. E.|last2=Tannenbaum|first2=M.|title=Superconducting Magnets|journal=Scientific American|date=June 1962|volume=206|issue=6|pages=60–67|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0662-60|bibcode=1962SciAm.206f..60K|url=https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1395472/|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Tanenbaum and Kunzler's group created the first high-field superconducting magnets, showing that Nb3Sn exhibits superconductivity at large currents and strong magnetic fields. Nb3Sn became the first known material suitable for use in high-powered magnets and electric machinery.<ref name="geballe">{{cite journal|last = Geballe|first = Theodore H.|authorlink = Theodore H. Geballe|title = Superconductivity: From Physics to Technology|journal = [[Physics Today]]|volume = 46|issue = 10|year = 1993|pages = 52–56|doi = 10.1063/1.881384|bibcode = 1993PhT....46j..52G}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal = [[Supercond. Sci. Technol.]]|volume = 19|issue = 8|pages = R68&ndash;R80|year = 2006|title = A review of the properties of Nb3Sn and their variation with A15 composition, morphology and strain state|first = A.|last = Godeke|doi = 10.1088/0953-2048/19/8/R02|arxiv = cond-mat/0606303|bibcode = 2006SuScT..19R..68G|s2cid = 73655040}}</ref> Their discovery made possible the eventual development of [[medical imaging]] devices.<ref name="Friedman"/>

Tanenbaum eventually moved from research into management, a change in focus that some speculate may have cost him a [[Nobel Prize]].<ref name="Friedman"/>

== Death ==
Tanenbaum died in his home in [[New Providence, New Jersey]], on February 26, 2023.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hagerty |first=James R. |date=March 4, 2023 |title=Morris Tanenbaum, Who Helped Put Silicon in Microchips, Dies at 94 |language=en-US |work=The Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/morris-tanenbaum-who-helped-put-silicon-in-microchips-dies-at-94-423f9f1c |access-date=2023-03-05}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
In 1962, Tanenbaum became a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]].<ref name="APS">{{cite web|title=APS Fellow Archive|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=&unit_id=&institution=Bell+Telephone+Laboratories|website=American Physical Society|access-date=11 February 2018}}</ref>

In 1970, he became a fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE).<ref name="OH"/>
In 1972, Tanenbaum was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]], for "Achievements in solid state research and technology and in technology transfer from research to manufacturing."<ref name="NAE">{{cite web|title=Dr. Morris Tanenbaum |url=https://www.nae.edu/MembersSection/MemberDirectory/28472.aspx|website=National Academy of Engineering|access-date=9 February 2018}}</ref>
In 1984 he received the [[IEEE Centennial Medal]].<ref name="OH"/>

In 1990 Tanenbaum became a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (AAAS).<ref>{{cite web|title=Members of the American Academy of Arts & Sciences: 1780-2012|url=https://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterT.pdf|website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences|page=534|access-date=13 February 2018}}</ref>
In 1996 he became a life member of the [[MIT Corporation]], the board of trustees of [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="MIT">{{cite web|title=Morris Tanenbaum|url=https://corporation.mit.edu/all-members/morris-tanenbaum|website=The MIT Corporation|access-date=9 February 2018}}</ref><ref name="OH"/> He received multiple honorary doctorates.<ref name="OH"/>

In 2013, Tanenbaum received a lifetime achievement award, the Science and Technology Medal, at the 34th Edison Patent Awards which are given by the [[Research & Development Council of New Jersey]].<ref name="Friedman"/>
